newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Baltic premiers say ready to start EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Baltic premiers say ready to start EU talks.

text.p: The prime ministers of the three Baltic states jointly declared their readiness on Thursday to start talks on joining the European Union (EU).
They made the statement as the EU prepares to lay the groundwork for expansion eastwards at a summit in Amsterdam next week.

"We expressed the mutual opininion that all the Baltic countries are ready to start negotiations," Estonian Prime Minister Mart Siimann said after meeting Latvian leader Andris Shkele and Lithuanian Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius.
Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia want to join the EU, seeing membership of the bloc as the best way to throw off the burden of 50 years as unwilling members of the Soviet empire.
After regaining independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991, all three have made great strides in transforming into market economies and rebuilding ties with the West.
"Secondly, we agree that objective criteria must be taken into account," Siimann added.
The Baltic states worry they will not be judged on economic success alone when the EU admits new members.
Estonia and Latvia have border rows with Russia and hundreds of thousands of ethnic Russian speakers live on their territory, most of whom are not citizens of these countries.
Siimann said he did not think geo-political factors would dominate when decisions were made on EU entrants.
Tiny Estonia, with a population of just 1.5 million, is seen as the economic and reform leader of the Baltic states.
Some analysts say the EU should admit at least one Baltic state as a reward for their commitment to reform and that should be Estonia.
"Estonia's standpoint is that if one or two Baltic countries are admitted in the first row, then all the Baltic countries will gain," Siimann said.

Nordic EU members voice strong support for Baltic entry but leading nations such as Germany and France, while sympathetic to the Baltic states, have appeared more concerned to secure entry for central European states such as Poland and the Czech Republic.
